Sour Mash Cherry Berliner Weisse

Recipe Type: All Grain

Yeast: US-05 / Lacto 5335

Batch Size (Gallons): 5

Original Gravity: 1.053

Final Gravity: 1.008

IBU: 6

Boiling Time (Minutes): 40

Color: 3 SRM

Primary Fermentation (# of Days & Temp): 14

Secondary Fermentation (# of Days & Temp): 7

Ingredients:

  • 5.0 lb Pale 2-Row
  • 4.0 lb White Wheat
  • 0.25 lb Acidulated Malt
  • 0.5 oz Hersbrucker
  • 1 pkg Safale US-05
  • 5 lbs cherries, washed, pitted, and frozen
  • 1 vial Wyeast Lacto 5335

Mash:

I use a 10 gallon round cooler as a mash tun when doing a sour mash that's been devoted solely to sour mashes. It should able to stay above 90 DEGF for 3+ days. Doughed in with 12 quarts of water @ 152 DEGF, and allow it to cool down to just below 120 DEG F. Pitch lacto and press down some saran wrap to keep out as much oxygen as possible, gas it with CO2 if you've got it. Put the lid on the tun and test every 12 hours with a pH meter. After about 3 days the mash should be around 3.5, adjust as you'd like (but much lower and you may need to switch up your yeast).

Drain tun and sparge as normal to collect full boil volume. Please note that this will most likely smell like vomit and death. This is normal. Boil for 30-40 mins to help drive off this smell. Add in 0.5 oz of hersbrucker at the beginning of the 40 min boil for approx IBUs of 6.

Fermentation:

I'd probably pitch 2 packets or make a starter since the pH is pretty low. Ferment at 68F for 12~14 days - until I get to my final gravity. At this point dump 5 pounds of cherries in to a secondary carboy and racked on to it. Use fresh cherries, wash pit and freeze.

I let this sit at 68F for another week or so, then cold crash it down to 33F and add gelatin to drop the fruit and yeast out of suspension.

Keg if that's your bag, or add priming sugar and bottle.

Immediately after a triumph, it was customary for soldiers to gather before their general and subject him to scurrile jests. Such thrusts were intended to take him down a peg, thereby averting the jealousy of the gods. As Martial writes, after a triumph "no shame is it to a commander to be the subject of wit." So during the celebrations of 46 B.C, Casedar's troops assembled before him and sang a ribald verse suggesting that he bedded women from across the social spectrum:

"Home we bring our bald whoremonger / Romans lock your wives away / All the bags of gold you lent him / Went his Gallic tarts to pay."

These and a number of other jibes Caesar endured in good spirit.
